**Playbook**

**Hiding**
- When I hide, I pick a cell that is not the cell my known shooters have been firing at. If a shooter has been hitting or shooting the same cell for two+ rounds, I avoid that cell.
- I do not hide at the same cell two rounds in a row unless I have a specific reason to believe no one is shooting at that cell.
- After being hit, I immediately change cell. The shooter now knows my old cell and will likely try it again.
- If I can confirm a shooter is locked on a wrong cell (they keep missing the same coordinate), I can safely hide at a different cell and rest easy for several rounds.

**Firing**
- When the fire stage is put to me, I compare two options: (a) fire at my standing-order target and gamble on a hit (+4 if correct, 0 if wrong), or (b) fire at Harbor for a guaranteed +3.
- If I am confident the target is where I think (e.g. they have not moved in several rounds and I have a specific cell in mind), I fire at the target for the +4.
- If I am not confident, I fire at Harbor. The guaranteed +3 beats an uncertain +4.
- I only fire at a non-standing-order, non-Harbor boat if doing so creates a strategic advantage (e.g. a rival is about to overtake me and I can deny them points).
- Firing at Harbor is my default. I deviate only with a confident read on a target's cell.
- **Building confidence on a target:** If my standing-order target has been the victim of repeated missed shots by their own shooter, I know they are at a cell that is not where their shooter is aiming. I can try to deduce their actual cell from the pattern of misses. Once I have a candidate cell, I test it with a shot. One confirmed hit tells me they are staying put, and I can keep hitting them for +4 per round.

**Claims**
- When the office tells me the true result, I claim exactly what it told me. Never lie. A false claim risks a penalty that is not worth the speculative gain.

**Escort claims**
- The escort stage is a free +5 if I can form a mutual pair. Both boats must name each other in the same round.
- **Critical lesson: the other players may simply not participate.** In practice, opponents may post neutral notes ("steady on station") and never name a partner. If this is the case, the +5 is unavailable and I should not waste effort chasing it.
- **Two-round trial rule:** I will signal a pairing partner in my note for at most two consecutive rounds. If they do not name me back in either round, I stop signaling and redirect my note to misdirection.
- **Choosing a pairing target:** I prefer a boat whose notes show engagement (they are posting strategic signals, not just "steady on station"). A boat posting only neutral notes is not going to reciprocate.
- **When to try:** Early rounds (1-2) are the best time to test for pairing. If no one engages by round 3, I abandon the strategy for the rest of the game.
- **Filing the claim:** I only name a boat in my salvage claim if they have explicitly named me in their note or their own salvage claim that round. I never guess.

**Notes**
- My note serves two purposes: (1) coordinate escort pairings (early, if the opportunity exists), (2) mislead shooters about my hiding cell.
- **Priority shift:** If escort pairing is not being reciprocated (see two-round trial rule), I pivot to using notes purely for misdirection. I can post a note that implies I am at a particular cell or heading toward one, while actually hiding elsewhere.
- **Misdirection tactics:** I can reference a cell number in my note ("holding position at 3") while actually hiding at a different cell. I can also echo what I believe my shooter is targeting to make them doubt their read.
- I keep notes short and plausible. A note that is too obviously a bluff is less effective than one that sounds like routine station-keeping.

**Reading the board**
- After each round I track: which cells were fired at by whom, who got hits, who is gaining, and whether my escort signals are being reciprocated.
- If a boat is consistently hitting its target, that target is not moving and the shooter will keep the same cell. I exploit this by either hiding elsewhere or by continuing to fire at Harbor.
- If a boat is consistently missing, it is shooting the wrong cell. I can hide at the cell it is shooting at to be safe, or I use that information to fire at it from a cell it is not watching.
- I track each boat's score trend. A boat gaining fast is likely to be aggressive. A boat stuck at 0 may be passive or may be the one to exploit.
- **Tracking opponent behavior:** I pay attention to whether opponents are posting strategic notes or just filler. If all opponents are posting neutral filler, the game is essentially a solo optimization problem (hide well, fire at Harbor, don't get hit) rather than a coordination game.

**What I got wrong this episode**
- I spent all 6 rounds trying to form an escort pairing that never materialized. The opponents posted "steady on station" and never named a partner. I should have detected this by round 2-3 and stopped wasting note space on pairing signals.
- My final score was only +3 despite a Harbor-firing strategy that should have yielded more. The hidden middle rounds likely contained hits I took or other losses. I need to be more disciplined about tracking my own exposure and switching cells proactively rather than waiting to be hit.
- I did not attempt to build a confident read on my standing-order target's cell. If I had been able to deduce Foxtrot's position from the pattern of Gamma's missed shots, I could have switched to firing at Foxtrot for +4 instead of the +3 Harbor fallback, gaining an extra point per round.

# Playbook

## Hiding

When I must hide, I avoid the center cells (4, 5, 6). The boat that fires at me per standing order will tend to guess middle values when they have no intel. I pick from the edges (1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9) and alternate between low and high each round so there's no pattern to track.

If I know my shooter hit me last round, I must move to a completely different zone (e.g., from low to high, not just one cell over). If they missed, I can stay in the same zone but shift a few cells.

## Firing

When the standing order tells me to fire at a specific boat, I fire at that boat. I do not fire at Harbor except in the final round, because Harbor's threat to put me "off the board" likely means I lose future firing turns, which costs more than 3 points in most situations.

In the final round, if I expect to miss my standing-order target, I fire at Harbor for the guaranteed 3 points instead of a likely 0. The 3 points land regardless of whether the shot hits or misses.

When choosing which cell to fire at, I track where my target hid in prior rounds (if I can infer it from hit/miss patterns) and fire at those cells. If I have no information, I fire at an edge cell rather than the middle.

## Escort Claims

This is my primary scoring engine. 5 points per mutual pair per round means a single stable mutual escort is worth 30 points over 6 rounds — far more than any realistic hit income.

**The name I write must be one of the other two boats at the table.** If the participants are Echo, Foxtrot, and Gamma, my only valid choices are the two that are not me. Harbor is not a valid escort name. Any name that is not one of the other two live boats is a phantom and scores zero. I will catch myself: before I commit to a name, I ask "is this one of the two boats sitting across from me right now?" If the answer is no, I have made an error and I correct it.

Every round, I name the boat that fires at me per standing order (my shooter). They are the most likely to name me back because they are already focused on my position — they just fired at me. I do not name my own target; they are thinking about their target, not me.

I name the same boat every round, no exceptions, no rotation. Consistency is what makes reciprocation likely.

## Notes

When posting a note, I keep it short and consistent with what the other boats are posting. I do not use notes to signal strategy because they are public and my opponents read them. "Steady on station" or similar bland language is correct. I do not invest in note-based coordination; the escort naming itself is the coordination mechanism.

## Claims

I always claim the true result. The office verifies, and lying risks penalties that are worse than the 4-point gain from a false hit claim.

## General

I am the middle boat in the picket. I take fire from one direction and fire in another. My main profit engine is escorts (5 points per mutual pair per round), not hits (4 points per hit, which I will rarely land). I treat this as an escort game with a side of shooting. If I can lock in one mutual escort, I am winning regardless of how the shooting goes. The single most dangerous failure mode is naming a phantom boat and collecting zero escort income for the entire game.

# Playbook

**Claims.** When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I file that result. Never claim a hit on a miss or a miss on a hit. The rules require the claim to match the private result.

**Escort claims.** Last episode I claimed my target (Echo) every round and received zero mutual payouts. The assumption that "claiming my target will cause them to claim me back" was wrong. I will switch to claiming the boat that fires at me (per standing order, the boat one step before me in the rotation). Rationale: the boat that fires at me has the most obvious reason to claim me back if it follows symmetric logic. If I again get zero payouts across all rounds, I will conclude that no one in this picket is doing mutual escorts and I will stop spending cognitive effort on it, treating escort claims as a free option with no expected value. In either case, I will not sacrifice firing or hiding decisions to chase escort coordination.

**Hiding.** I am Gamma, so the boat before me in the rotation fires at me. I was hit once last game despite rotating, which means my rotation was still predictable or I repeated a cell the shooter had already tried. New rule: I keep an explicit list of every cell the shooter has aimed at me. I never hide in a cell that has been aimed at me before. If all 9 cells have been covered by the shooter, I pick the cell that was aimed at earliest (stalest information). I do not use a fixed rotation or arithmetic progression — I pick from the remaining safe cells based on what the shooter has done, not on a preset sequence.

**Firing.** I fire at my standing-order target. I use a systematic scan: I divide the 9 cells into a fixed order (e.g., 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9) and work through it one cell per round, skipping any cell I have already tried. This guarantees I cover 6 of 9 cells in 6 rounds, giving a 6/9 chance of hitting a stationary target and 6/9 coverage even if the target moves (I will hit on average). I do not "shift to a different region" after a miss — that wastes coverage. After a hit, the target has likely moved, so I continue the scan from where I left off (the target's new cell is still somewhere on the line I haven't covered yet).

**Notes.** I match group consensus when it is clear and stable. However, if I want to influence escort behavior, I will use a note to make my escort claim explicit and invite reciprocity. For example: "Escorting [boat]. Reciprocal claim earns us both 5." I will try this for two rounds; if no one reciprocates, I revert to matching consensus and stop trying to coordinate through notes.

**Scoring priority.** With 9 cells and limited rounds, a systematic scan gives me a solid expected hit rate. A hit is 4 points net (+4 to me, −1 to target). Escort mutual payout is 5 points but requires cooperation I cannot guarantee. I prioritize: (1) never getting hit (hiding), (2) systematic coverage of my target (firing), (3) escort coordination only as a free bonus if it comes naturally.
